subtitle: Word families and their endings, and words for everyone
words.intro: No subject fills a German Sunday lunch, a radio phone-in and a letters page quite like the ending of a word. Can you say *Studenten* any more? Should you say *Studierende*? People have fallen out over less, and you may be asked.

grammar[0].fact: From one verb, German can build a family: *führen, durchführen, durchführbar, die Durchführbarkeit*, and *undurchführbar*. Each one is real, and a report may well use them all. In speech, you could just say *Das geht nicht*.

grammar[1].fact: *Die Eltern* has no singular, *die Leute* neither, and *das Gepäck* no plural. German grammar has had three genders for a thousand years, and it still calls a girl *das Mädchen*, which is one of the very few things that all sides in the debate agree is odd.

document.intro: A real notice from a parish office, taped to a door in the pandemic. It’s short and polite, and in its first line there’s the star. Nobody here is making a point: it’s how this office writes now.
document.fact: The notice is a good sample of what you’ll actually meet: not a debate but a form of address. And look at *Aufgrund der gestiegenen Infektionszahlen*, a nominal phrase of the kind you’ll practise in chapter 8.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Write the same address another way.
reading.intro: Jonas has finally got a job, as an assistant in a university’s press office. On his first day, he has to write one sentence to everyone: the canteen will close on Friday. By half past nine he has had seven replies, and no one has mentioned the canteen.
reading.photos[1].caption: Eine Vorlesung: alle Formen, voll besetzt.
reading.fact: This one is really disputed, and you’ll meet all the forms: *Studentinnen und Studenten*, *Studierende*, *Student:innen*, *Student*innen*. Some states have banned the star in schools and offices, and some universities encourage it. You needn’t have an opinion. You do need to read all of them.
